name: David Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello David, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: David, 27. I rent a flat with a mate from school, Ollie, who works in a bike shop. I left school at sixteen, did a bit of everything, and I've been at the warehouse ten months. On the side I buy and resell trainers online, limited releases mostly, and that's been good to me. Between that and the warehouse wage I've got about a year of costs saved and some money in shares.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The warehouse is a logistics company that stores and ships for a few sports brands, so football boots, gym kit, tracksuits. I pick from shelves with a scanner, put it into cartons and send it down a conveyor. There are a couple of robot arms on the packing end, and a self-driving cart that follows you round, which I love. I'm not quick yet, my rate's in the bottom third. I like the gadgets and the people. I don't like the sorting in peak season when we're on twelve-hour days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That'd be a bit of a letdown, honestly. I use AI for half my side business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a good tool that got oversold. I'd post something about how I still use it every day for my listings. At work I'd say we've got the same jobs and slightly better gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think it's fine. My warehouse job stays, and my trainer side thing keeps ticking over with AI writing my listings and checking prices. Nothing to complain about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep growing the reselling, maybe aim for an extra 400 a month. I'd keep putting a bit into shares every payday. Maybe I'd look at the team leader route in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, actually. I like my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the routine stuff AI does for you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI writes my listings, suggests a price from recent sales, and saves me maybe an hour a night. It also tells me which releases are worth queuing for. That's enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any pressure in your life that AI doesn't touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, mainly. It's gone up twice in two years. I could buy somewhere with what I've got, but I like having the money free to flip trainers.

say: I'd say AI was a **good tool** that got **oversold**.
I'd post that I still use it **every day** for my listings.
think: My **warehouse job** stays and the **trainer reselling** keeps ticking over.
AI saves me about **an hour a night**, which is enough.
do: Grow the **reselling** by about **400 a month**.
Put some money into **shares** every payday.
Look at the **team leader** route in a couple of years.
feel: **Calm** and fairly happy with his life.
S0.quote: AI writes my listings, suggests a price from recent sales, and saves me maybe an hour a night.
fieldNote: He's the only one in his warehouse who treats AI as a **business partner**.
His **side income** and shares make him unusually secure for a junior.
**Rent rises** are the one pressure he names.

steps.text: Grow the trainer reselling by about 400 a month
Put money into shares every payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying, checking, answering customers, that's basically my side business. Interesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, not doom, and you just have to get on it early. I'd probably post tips on how I use AI for selling. At work I'd tell people to learn the new systems before they're forced to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think my warehouse job is all right, but my side thing gets crowded. If everyone has AI finding underpriced trainers, the bargains disappear. So the bit of my income I thought was clever becomes ordinary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shift the reselling towards something harder to copy, like cleaning and restoring old trainers, which needs hands. I'd sign up for whatever training the warehouse offers on the new robots. I'd keep investing, maybe a bit more in companies that make the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about the warehouse, more about the side money drying up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Restoring trainers is quite a change. Where did that idea come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ollie does bike repairs, and he's always saying people pay for hands. I've watched videos, it's brushes, glue and paint. Machines can't do a nice job on a 1990s pair yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put more effort into the warehouse in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I'd try to get on the robot side, the people who look after the arms and the carts. It's better paid and it looks like where the jobs go.

say: I'd say it's **change, not doom**, and you have to get on it early.
I'd post **tips** on using AI for selling.
think: My **warehouse job** is all right, but my side business gets crowded.
If everyone's AI finds cheap trainers, the **bargains disappear**.
do: Shift reselling towards **restoring old trainers**, which needs hands.
Sign up for **robot training** at the warehouse.
Invest a bit more in **robot-making companies**.
feel: **Uneasy** about the **side money** drying up, not the warehouse job.
S1.quote: If everyone has AI finding underpriced trainers, the bargains disappear.
fieldNote: He sees **thinking AI** hitting his side business before his main job.
His answer is to move towards **hands-on craft** in the side business.
He looks at the **robot team** as the next step in the warehouse.

steps.text: Switch the side business to restoring old trainers by hand

Put extra savings into companies that make warehouse robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028 for AGI, 2031 for robots. Okay, that's a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be wild, and we need a plan from the government, not just from tech firms. I'd keep it calm-ish online. At work I'd tell people to save money now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my warehouse job's gone by 2031, and the online side gone by 2028, because AI does all the buying and selling better than me. My shares might do well if I picked right, but that's a guess. So I'd be leaning on my savings and figuring out what's left for humans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move straight into the robot maintenance team for the extra pay while it lasts. I'd put more into shares in the companies building this stuff. I'd grow the restoring side, because even with AI someone has to scrub the glue. And I'd keep a year of costs in cash and not touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not falling apart, but my plan has holes everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your shares might do well. Is that a plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both, if I'm honest. I'm not an expert, I watch videos. But if robots replace workers, the people who own the robots win, and I'd rather own a tiny bit of that than none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ollie?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mate Ollie to keep fixing bikes, because hands-on repair lasts longest. Then I'd ask if he wants to share a workshop. Half joking.

say: I'd say we need a **government plan**, not just one from tech firms.
I'd tell colleagues to **save money now**.
think: My **warehouse job** goes by 2031 and the **online side** by 2028.
Shares might do well, but that's **a guess**, so savings carry me.
do: Move into **robot maintenance** straight away for extra pay.
Put more into **shares** in companies building AI and robots.
Keep **a year of costs** in cash, untouched.
S2.quote: If robots replace workers, the people who own the robots win, and I'd rather own a tiny bit of that than none.
fieldNote: He sees **both incomes** at risk: thinking AI takes the side business first.
He hedges by **owning shares** in the companies doing the replacing.
He admits his share plan is **part hope**.

steps.text: Move into the robot maintenance team straight away

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 then 2034. Seven years for the warehouse. That's a decent run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so the smart move is to learn the new stuff early. I'd post about it like a challenge, not a disaster. At work I'd be the one showing people the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think that's enough time to build something. Maintenance work for five or six years, savings growing, shares hopefully growing, and the restoring business as a side thing. I'd still end up needing a new plan in my mid-thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get into robot maintenance within the year. I'd build the restoring business properly, with a small website and a workbench in Ollie's shop. And I'd keep investing every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a cliff out there, but I can see it, and I've got time to build a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'a bridge' look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money in the bank, a skill with my hands, and some shares: if one breaks, I've still got two. Three legs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone who'd be hurt more than you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Loads of the lads at work. Most don't save, they live payday to payday. I'd try to get them to put even 50 a month away, but you can't force people.

say: I'd say the **smart move** is to learn the new stuff early.
I'd post about it as a **challenge**, not a disaster.
think: Seven years is enough to **build something** before the robots arrive.
I'd still need a **new plan** in my mid-thirties.
do: Get into **robot maintenance** within the year.
Build the **restoring business** with a small website and a workbench.
feel: **Uneasy**, seeing a **cliff** ahead but with time to build a bridge.
S3.quote: Money in the bank, a skill with my hands, and some shares: if one breaks, I've still got two.
fieldNote: His safety plan has **three legs**: savings, hands-on skill and shares.
He worries for **colleagues** who live payday to payday.
Five years of warning lets him **build** instead of scramble.

steps.text: Get into robot maintenance within the year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots by 2039. That's ages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best case, everyone gets time to adapt. I'd still tell people to start learning now. I'd probably be a bit of a bore about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I'm fine. I'd have a decade to build up money, maybe buy a flat, get qualified on the robots. By the time robots do hands-on work, I'd want to own something, not work for someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI every day for the side business and for studying robotics basics. I'd keep investing and maybe buy a flat in a few years. I'd go for the maintenance team when a spot opens, not rush it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Even a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 'own something' look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a small shop that restores trainers and bikes with Ollie. Or a share in a business that rents out robots to small warehouses. I don't know yet, I've got ten years to figure it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you less calm in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the government did nothing for ten years and then panicked. Then it's the fast picture again, just later.

say: I'd say a decade is the **best case**, with time for everyone to adapt.
I'd still nag people to **start learning** now.
think: I'm **fine**: a decade to build money and get **qualified on robots**.
By 2039 I'd want to **own something**, not work for someone.
do: Use **AI every day** for the side business and studying robotics.
Keep **investing** and maybe buy a **flat** in a few years.
Join the **maintenance team** when a spot opens.
S4.quote: By the time robots do hands-on work, I'd want to own something, not work for someone.
fieldNote: Long notice turns him towards **owning a business**.
His one fear is a **government that waits** and then panics.
He treats **AI** as a study tool, unusual among his colleagues.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because both my incomes go at once. What would help is cheap training on the robots for people already on the floor, and a clear plan from the government so it's not a scramble.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about owning things. If machines do the work, the question is who owns the machines. I'd like ordinary people to own a bit of it.

headlineQuote: If machines do the work, the question is who owns the machines.
portrait: David is a **27-year-old picker** at a sports goods logistics warehouse, and he loves the gadgets.
He resells trainers online with **AI tools**, has a year saved and owns some **shares**.
He sees thinking AI hitting his **side business** before his warehouse job.
His plan rests on **three legs**: cash, hands-on restoring skills and shares.
With ten years' warning he dreams of **owning a business**, not working for someone.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his warehouse and online incomes would go together.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **government plan** to avoid a scramble.
